text: This lab puts the last three lessons to work on one real rollout: an Employee Service Center going out across eight departments, funded by stakeholders who genuinely want different things from it. You're the Technical Architect asked to make it real.

Finance needs every request to pass through a tight, auditable approval chain, because some request types touch regulated spend. Marketing wants fast, near-frictionless self-service, because its volume is high and its real approval risk is low. Centralized governance forces both through the same review queue, which either over-controls Marketing or under-controls Finance. The real choice is federated governance, with Lesson 25's guardrails actively enforced across all eight departments: one naming convention, mandatory code review, and a shared component library so nobody rebuilds the intake experience from scratch.

Lesson 26's sequencing rule picks the pilot: Marketing, not Finance, because its use case is simplest, not because it's the biggest department. A clean pilot win there builds the confidence that makes Finance's harder, higher-stakes rollout land smoothly afterward. The base intake form, data model, and notification framework get built once as the shared piece every department uses. Approval routing is where departments genuinely differ, so Marketing's extension routes requests straight through, and Finance's extension adds the multi-step chain its compliance need actually requires — neither forking the shared base to get there.

Presenting this to the CFO and department heads means Lesson 27's translation, not the technical vocabulary: every department gets a request experience built once, so nobody's paying to build eight separate systems. Marketing gets speed because its real risk is low; Finance keeps the approval chain its compliance need actually requires; a small shared platform team keeps standards consistent across all eight so nothing gets rebuilt twice.

Same governance model, same shared-versus-specific line, same real cost and risk — just framed in terms the room holding the budget can actually evaluate and defend the next time someone questions it.
That closes Chapter Eight. Chapter Nine opens with the course's final scenario: a full capstone kickoff, applying everything built across all eight chapters to a 5,000-employee organization.
